chapter.name: Beyond Earth
chapter.blurb: Stars form patterns called constellations (now officially 88 sky regions defined by the IAU); night sky visibility depends on light pollution and location. The Solar System has the Sun, eight planets (inner rocky, outer gas/ice giants), the Moon and other natural satellites, asteroids and comets. The Solar System is part of the Milky Way Galaxy, itself one of many galaxies in the Universe.

scope_in.item: Stars shine with their own light; groups of stars forming patterns were historically called constellations, used for storytelling and navigation; the IAU officially divided the sky into 88 constellations (defined regions) in the early 20th century; example constellations Orion, Taurus, Canis Major (containing Sirius, the brightest star), Ursa Major (Big Dipper) and Ursa Minor (Little Dipper, containing the Pole Star)

Night sky watching: light pollution (excessive artificial light) and obstructions reduce star visibility; not all stars/constellations are visible from every location (e.g. the Pole Star is not visible from the southern hemisphere) or every night; locating the Pole Star using the Big Dipper's cup stars (about five times their separation); locating Orion via its three-star belt, and Sirius via a line through Orion's belt

The Sun: a star, the closest to Earth, a hot ball of gases, source of Earth's heat/light/energy, about 100 times Earth's diameter, about 150 million km away (roughly 1 astronomical unit); a planet is a large, nearly spherical object revolving around the Sun; Earth rotates on its axis in about 24 hours (a day) and revolves around the Sun in about a year

The eight planets in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune; inner four are smaller/rocky, outer four are larger/made of gas and ice with rings; Mars is the Red Planet, Earth is the Blue Planet, Venus is the Morning/Evening Star; Venus is hotter than Mercury due to its atmosphere; stars twinkle, planets generally do not; Pluto is now a dwarf planet, not one of the eight planets, per the IAU's 2006 redefinition

Natural satellites: objects moving around planets; the Moon is Earth's natural satellite, taking about 27 days to revolve around Earth, about a quarter of Earth's diameter, with hardly any atmosphere so its craters (from asteroid/rock impacts) persist for a very long time; Earth has 1 moon, Mars has 2, the outer giant planets have many; India's Chandrayaan-1 (2008), Chandrayaan-2 (2019) and Chandrayaan-3 (2023, successful soft landing near the Moon's south pole, marked as National Space Day on 23 August) missions; planned Chandrayaan-4 aims to bring back Moon samples

Asteroids: small, rocky, irregularly shaped objects, mostly in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, sized roughly 10 m to 500 km; comets: icy-rocky objects from the outer Solar System that develop a tail as they approach the Sun and their frozen material evaporates, some revolving periodically, some escaping or breaking up/falling into the Sun or a planet; Halley's Comet appears about every 76 years (last seen 1986)

The Solar System comprises the Sun, eight planets, their moons, asteroids and comets; the Sun is the largest/heaviest object and produces almost all the Solar System's energy, other objects shine by reflecting sunlight; the Milky Way Galaxy is our home galaxy (visible as a faint band on a dark, moonless night), containing millions to billions of stars, of which our Solar System is a small part; the Universe contains many galaxies beyond the Milky Way; scientists search for life mainly via exoplanets, with no confirmed evidence found so far

concepts.name: Stars and constellations
concepts.description: Constellations were historically star patterns and are now officially defined sky regions (88, per the IAU), used historically for storytelling and navigation.
concepts.idea: A constellation is a group of stars that appears to form a pattern, though today the term officially refers to a defined region of the sky.
concepts.rule: The IAU officially divided the entire sky into 88 constellations in the early twentieth century; Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky.
concepts.example: Orion, pictured as a hunter with a three-star belt, is a well-known constellation; the Big Dipper (Ursa Major) and Little Dipper (Ursa Minor, containing the Pole Star) are two other recognisable patterns.

questions.a: This claim is not fully accurate. s: States the claim is not fully accurate/needs qualification

concepts.name: Night sky watching: light pollution and locating objects
concepts.description: Star visibility depends on darkness and clear conditions; light pollution and location affect what can be seen, and specific methods help locate the Pole Star, Orion and Sirius.
concepts.idea: The number of visible stars depends on how dark and clear the sky is; light pollution and obstructions reduce visibility, so open, dark areas are best.
concepts.rule: Not all stars/constellations are visible from every place or night; the Pole Star is not visible from the southern hemisphere; the Big Dipper's cup stars, extended about five times their separation, help locate the Pole Star.
concepts.example: Cities show fewer stars due to light pollution, smoke and dust; Orion is best viewed in India December to April after sunset, its three-star belt being the easiest way to identify it.

concepts.name: The Sun and the planets of the Solar System

concepts.idea: The Sun is a star, an extremely hot ball of glowing gases and the closest star to Earth; a planet is a large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun.
concepts.rule: The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune; the inner four are smaller and rocky, the outer four are larger, made of gas/ice, with rings; stars twinkle, planets generally do not.
concepts.example: Mars is the Red Planet due to reddish soil; Earth is the Blue Planet due to its water; Venus is the Morning/Evening Star though it is a planet; Venus is hotter than Mercury because its atmosphere traps heat.
